title: The Scholar Who Had Read Everything
hookLine: a well-known scholar climbs to a silent young sage with one question
carry: jnana: know the knower, not just the facts
tomorrow: 'it was meant to be' or 'you made it happen'? which?

lines: I'VE READ EVERYTHING. I STILL DON'T KNOW.
cards: 1907, the hill at Tiruvannamalai. A man climbs to a cave where a young sage sits, mostly in silence.

The climber is well-known: Ganapati Muni, a Sanskrit poet so gifted people called him Kavyakantha, the one with poetry in his throat. He has read the scriptures, studied Vedanta, repeated his mantras for years.
And he falls at the young man's feet and says, roughly: I've read everything there is to read. I still don't understand what tapas, real spiritual practice, is. Teach me.

teach.h: WATCH WHERE THE I SPRINGS: TAPAS.
teach.b: The young sage, Ramana, looks at him in silence for a long while. Then he answers, in the account his followers keep: watch where the thought I springs from, and the mind sinks back into it. That is tapas.
And when you repeat a mantra, watch where its sound rises, and the mind sinks there too. Ganapati Muni went down the hill and gave the young man the name he's known by: Bhagavan Sri Ramana Maharshi.
Here's the teaching under the story, and it's an old one.
The Mundaka Upanishad says there are two kinds of knowing. The lower is all learning, and its list even includes the Vedas themselves.
The higher is the knowing by which the imperishable is known. Hindus call that higher knowing jnana, and its opposite ajnana. Ramana's Forty Verses turn it into a puzzle.

In paraphrase: knowledge and ignorance come as a pair, each needing the other; to know whose knowledge and ignorance they are, that is real knowledge. Learn one more fact and the not-knowing just shifts somewhere else.
So he steps off the seesaw and asks about the rider.

Then an image: rings and bangles have many shapes, but none stands apart from the gold. Knowledge of many things is like the shapes; the self that knows is like the gold. This isn't a case against study.
Ganapati Muni kept writing all his life. It's a question of order.
The greatest scholar on the hill still had to turn around and look at the knower.

how: Ramana's followers keep studying, and many sit the way he told Ganapati Muni: repeating a mantra, or asking 'who am I?', and watching where it rises.

o: a Tamil poem that asks who it is that knows
a set of school lessons in Sanskrit grammar

games.q: two kinds of knowing — tap the pairs.
p: watching where the I springs from

s: Ramana told Ganapati Muni to stop studying and burn his books
he pointed him to the knower; the Muni kept writing all his life.
the Mundaka Upanishad counts even the Vedas among the lower kind of knowing
the higher knowing is the one by which the imperishable is known.
in Ramana's image, the gold stands for the knower
the ornaments are knowledge of many things; the gold is the self that knows.

games.q: a friend cramming for finals says she'll be at peace once she knows everything on the syllabus. what would Ramana have told her, as he told the scholar?
o: study, and also turn to the one who knows: that's jnana.
she's right: total knowledge brings total peace.
she should stop studying, since facts don't matter.
games.why: the Upanishad's lower knowing is still knowing. the higher kind, jnana, is of the knower, and no syllabus covers it.

practice: If you have a mantra or a prayer you say, repeat it silently for the sit, slowly. If you don't pray, use Om, or simply your own name. Each time, notice where the sound seems to rise from, just before it's a word, and rest there.
That was Ramana's whole answer to the scholar.

wordCard.voice: Ramana's Forty Verses: a Tamil poem that asks, before anything else is known, who is knowing it.

orig.note: Sanskrit: knowledge; with a- in front, ajnana, not-knowing.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: jnana, know the knower, not just the facts. Many ornaments, and only ever the one gold.

sources.ref: Ganapati Muni's visit to Ramana at Virupaksha Cave, November 1907 (he had read all and done japa but did not know what tapas is; Ramana: watch where the notion 'I' springs from, and where the mantra's sound rises; that is tapas; the Muni names him Bhagavan Sri Ramana Maharshi)
sources.work: Arthur Osborne, Ramana Maharshi and the Path of Self-Knowledge (paraphrased)

sources.ref: Mundaka Upanishad 1.1.4–5 (two knowledges, higher and lower; the lower includes the four Vedas; the higher is that by which the imperishable is known)
Ulladu Narpadu, verses 10–11 (knowledge and ignorance depend on each other; knowing to whom they belong is real knowledge; knowing all else but not the knower)
sources.work: Ramana Maharshi, Ulladu Narpadu (Reality in Forty Verses) (paraphrased)
